props.title: Saved!

sections.content: Saved! brilliantly skewers Christian fundamentalism through dark comedy while maintaining genuine empathy for its characters' faith journeys. Like Election (1999) and Mean Girls (2004), it uses high school social dynamics to explore deeper themes. Mandy Moore delivers a standout performance as Hillary Faye, the zealous Christian popular girl whose certainty masks deep insecurity. The film tackles teenage pregnancy, sexuality, and religious hypocrisy with surprising nuance, joining films like Lady Bird (2017) and Easy A (2010) in examining the intersection of faith and coming-of-age.

sections.content: The early 2000s saw several films confronting religious fundamentalism through comedy and satire. A Mighty Wind (2003) and Thank God! (2022) use humor to examine blind faith, while documentaries like Hell House (2001) and For the Bible Tells Me So (2007) take more serious approaches to evangelical Christianity's impact on youth. Saved! stands out for maintaining warmth toward its characters while critiquing institutional rigidity.

The film's treatment of LGBTQ+ themes was groundbreaking for 2004, particularly in a movie centered on Christian teenagers. Like Love, Simon (2018) and Edge of Seventeen (2016), it presents queerness as natural and valid while acknowledging the very real struggles of coming out in conservative environments. The character of Patrick, played by Patrick Fugit, represents a more progressive Christianity that embraces questioning and inclusion. SUBHEAD: Faith and Teen Identity in Modern Cinema

sections.content: The film's legacy can be seen in later works like Yes, God, Yes (2019) and Eighth Grade (2018), which similarly explore teenage identity formation within restrictive religious environments. Director Brian Dannelly's decision to cast actual teenagers rather than twenty-somethings adds authenticity that echoes through contemporary coming-of-age films like Booksmart (2019) and The Edge of Seventeen (2016).
